reasoning: Both sets are thorough, single-package plans built on the same scaffolding, and both have good frozen interfaces. Set B teaches more RL: an ablation switch for each DQN part, a REINFORCE→actor-critic→PPO ladder, a taking-turns/simultaneous/self-play ladder with cross-play tables, and a corridor/line/chase set of test worlds that prove the core. But B is weaker as a build plan. Its M1 is training only, so nothing can be watched until M2. Every stage repeats the same train / baselines-curves-replay / study split. One 34-step PL-01 covers all three stages and is pasted into every packet. Task IDs run out of order (T20–T24 come before T14). The four DQN thicken tasks are chained one after another even though each writes its own file, and their Writes leave out agent.py, which the frozen-copy refresh and the ε schedule must change. The T16 packet doesn't give the targets.py seam signature. B also keeps stale text: the brief still says "The second environment, whatever it is", and the architecture still says "the build waits for … replan". Set A's M1 is a true walking skeleton (train a snake, record it, watch it). Its packets are tight and carry the frozen types and fakes they need, and its dependency graph is mostly sound, with real mitigations. A has its own faults: pipeline rows lag later decisions (train_ppo 'until the time limit' vs AD-18's step budget; load_policy 'torch.load the state dict' vs AD-15's GreedyNet; the steps still say the skills set the test and the chart when AD-20 and AD-21 now do), AD-22 contains process narration, and M3 is very large (both tank versions plus the SB3 check plus sign-off). Overall, A is the more buildable and more consistent plan.
